articles.title: Islam is 'greater' than other religions: Karnataka higher education minister Basavaraj Rayareddi
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Karnataka higher education minister Basavaraj Rayareddi on Sunday said Islam is \"greater\" than other religions, news agency PTI reported.He.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Karnataka higher education minister Basavaraj Rayareddi on Sunday said Islam is "greater" than other religions, news agency PTI reported.He expressed his desire to visit Mecca, but said he cannot do so as a non-Muslim.The minister made the remarks while speaking at a mass marriage programme for the Muslim community in Kuknoor in Koppal district.According to PTI, Rayareddi said, "I would like to say that Islam is shreshta dharam (great religion) than other dharmas...."He said there are misconceptions about the religion and added that he had tried to study the Quran, other religions and their history.Later, describing Islam as highly disciplined, highly scientific and the most humane religion, he said, "Read it, understand, and don't become bigots, don't become casteists. There are good and bad people in all religions, but bad things are always highlighted... We should respect all religions, we should know good things in all religions as religions are for well being of mankind and we should try to do good.""Islam is a good religion. I'm speaking here very happily. I'm thinking very much about going to Mecca, but I can't go there as one should convert to Islam (to go there). It's a tradition in that religion," he said."Islam is a good religion, there are good teachings in it, you should follow it, instead of just going to Masjid...," he added.His remarks drew a sharp reaction from BJP leader R Ashoka, who said that by stating, in effect, that "Islam is greater than other religions," Rayareddi had portrayed Sanatana Dharma in an inferior light.Ashoka, the leader of the opposition in the Assembly, demanded that Rayareddi withdraw his statements and apologise to all Hindus in the state.He also said that if Rayareddi refused, chief minister DK Shivakumar should demonstrate his commitment by removing him from the Cabinet."CM Shivakumar, is there no end to the anti-Hindu mindset of your Congress government? You go around visiting temples and putting on a display of devotion before cameras, but why do you remain silent when ministers in your own Cabinet make derogatory statements about Sanatana Hindu Dharma and temples," he asked.Ashoka further said, "... by stating, in effect, that Islam is greater than other religions, he has portrayed Sanatana Dharma in an inferior light."Questioning whether this was the Congress party's idea of "equal respect for all religions", Ashoka asked, "Is this your vision of a garden of peace for all communities? Or are all your theatrics and pretence merely another mask worn to secure Hindu votes?He said that if Rayareddi did not apologise or was not removed from the ministry, crores of Hindus in Karnataka would be left with one conclusion: "Your (CM) temple visits are not out of devotion. Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground and the North Kaibab Trail remain closed.The flood also damaged the Grand Canyon’s sole water pipeline, forcing the park to suspend overnight hotel stays from August 31 and ask residents to conserve water. articles.title: India's land records go digital: How maps, drones and Bhu-Aadhaar are changing property records
articles.summary: News News: Nearly every textual land record in India is now digital, with 99.90% of Records of Rights (RoRs) computerised. But how does a piece of land on the gr.
articles.body: Nearly every textual land record in India is now digital, with 99.90% of Records of Rights (RoRs) computerised. But how does a piece of land on the ground eventually get a digital identity?The answer lies in a mix of digitised maps, georeferencing and unique identification numbers for land parcels. The system was recently showcased to a high-level delegation from the African Union Commission, Ethiopia, Malawi, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Zambia, along with officials from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), during a visit to the Department of Land Resources (DoLR) in New Delhi.The delegation studied the Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme (DILRMP), Unique Land Parcel Identification Number (ULPIN), also called Bhu-Aadhaar, National Generic Document Registration System (NGDRS) and the NAKSHA programme for urban areas.From land records to digital identityOnce land records and maps are digitised, the government links the information to the actual location of the land.Around 76.16% of land parcels have been fully georeferenced, while 85.24% spatial-textual integration has been completed between cadastral maps and Records of Rights.India is also giving land parcels their own digital identity. More than 40.58 crore land parcels have been assigned a 14-digit alphanumeric identification number called Bhu-Aadhaar, or ULPIN.Department of Land Resources Secretary Narendra Bhooshan said Aadhaar had created India's digital identity layer and Bhu-Aadhaar was extending the same idea to land."Land is the largest and most foundational asset class in any developing economy. In traditional systems, without clear spatial titles and interoperability, vast amounts of land remain 'dead capital' that citizens cannot leverage.”He said the aim under DILRMP and the Bharat Land Stack was to build an "unshakeable digital trust architecture".“By linking georeferenced land records, circle rates, registration, and encumbrances into a single interoperable layer, we are creating an ecosystem where even the most vulnerable citizen or rural landowner can unlock formal credit and mortgages seamlessly. This experience and architecture are open to be shared with our partner nations across Africa to accelerate DPI-led inclusive growth across the Global South."What goes into the digital land map?A digital map of a property is not limited to its location and boundaries. India's Bharat Land Stack brings together several layers of land and property information.These include satellite and drone images, georeferenced cadastral boundaries, Records of Rights and property registration data. It also includes master plans and zoning rules, building approvals, restrictions and litigation, circle rates and tenancy details.The aim is to bring this information together on a single digital framework and create a common source for land-related information.The property registration system is also being digitised. Around 98.96% of Sub-Registrar Offices (SROs) have been computerised.Seventeen states and Union territories have adopted the centralised NGDRS platform, while 17 states use their own digital registration software.Information on property-related disputes is also being connected to land records. Around 94.11% of Revenue Courts have been computerised under the Revenue Court Case Management System (RCCMS), allowing litigation related to a property to be marked on its record in real time.Drones for mappingFor urban areas, India is using drones under the NAKSHA programme, or National Geospatial Knowledge-based Land Survey of Urban Habitations. DoLR Director (LR) Shyam Kumar explained the process to the visiting delegation.Drones fitted with 2D Nadir cameras, five-camera Oblique systems and LiDAR sensors are used to survey urban areas to achieve centimetre-level positional accuracy. The aerial surveys are used to create Ortho-Rectified Imagery (ORI), Digital Elevation Models (DEM) and 3D Reality Models, helping map complex urban landscapes.But the process does not end with the aerial survey as the data is checked on the ground using Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) GNSS rovers, along with participatory ground validation.There is also a claims and objections process to address issues raised during the mapping exercise.Under the NAKSHA pilot, aerial flying has been completed across 145 of 150 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs). The exercise has resulted in the issuance of legally authentic Urban Property (UrPro) Cards.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: A UK collector paid £62,000 for a mounted 'fox' head; X-rays revealed the skull of an extinct thylacine hidden inside
articles.summary: UK News: A mounted animal head that appeared to be little more than an old, poorly made fox has turned out to be something extraordinarily rare. British collec.
articles.body: A mounted animal head that appeared to be little more than an old, poorly made fox has turned out to be something extraordinarily rare. British collector James Cranfield paid £62,000 for the specimen at a UK auction after spotting a detail that other bidders had missed, its teeth did not belong to a fox. X-rays have now confirmed what Cranfield suspected. Hidden beneath the stuffing and taxidermy was an almost complete skull belonging to a thylacine, the extinct marsupial also known as the Tasmanian tiger. The discovery has transformed an obscure auction-house curiosity into a scientifically significant specimen. The skull is intact and in remarkably good condition, despite the exterior being described as a rather crude or “naive” mount. The specimen is now expected to be added to the International Thylacine Specimen Database, while scientists are also interested in obtaining DNA from it.How did a £40 'fox' turn out to be a thylacineThe head was originally entered into a general auction in the UK as a fox's head, with an estimated value of only about £30 to £50. Its unusual appearance, including plastic googly eyes and an exaggerated forehead, apparently did little to suggest that it might be one of the rarest taxidermy specimens in existence. Cranfield, however, runs an oddities shop and has spent much of his life collecting taxidermy and natural-history curiosities. When he examined the animal's teeth, he realised something was wrong with the auction description. The distinction came down to the number of incisors. Foxes and dogs have six upper incisors between their canines, while thylacines, as marsupials, have eight. According to BBC, Cranfield recognised the unusual dental arrangement and began comparing the specimen with known thylacine material. He was not the only bidder to realise what was hiding beneath the mount. Another dealer also recognised its significance, leading to a fierce bidding battle. Cranfield eventually secured it for £62,600 including auction fees, far above the original estimate. The head had reportedly been bought for just £50 at an antiques market before eventually being entered into the auction as a fox.X-rays exposed the extinct animal's skullAlthough the teeth had convinced Cranfield that the head was probably a thylacine, scientific confirmation was still needed. Radiographs have now provided that confirmation. The X-rays showed that the animal's skin had been stretched over a genuine, full skull rather than a replica or altered animal skeleton. According to ABC News, the skull is uncut and remarkably complete, with the radiographs clearly revealing its distinctive dentition. Steven Sleightholme, director of the International Thylacine Specimen Database, confirmed the identification after examining the radiographs. The database currently records 815 thylacine specimens worldwide, ranging from tiny pieces of tissue to complete mounts. The newly authenticated head is particularly unusual because there are believed to be only two known thylacine head mounts, making the discovery considerably more important than an ordinary taxidermy find. The specimen's lack of provenance means there are still unanswered questions about exactly where and when it was collected. Its age is believed to date to the late 19th century, but researchers hope further investigation may provide more information.Why does this thylacine specimen matter so much?The thylacine disappeared from the wild in Tasmania during the 20th century, with the last known individual dying at Beaumaris Zoo in Hobart on 7 September 1936. For decades, the species has remained one of the most famous examples of human-driven extinction. Its distinctive striped body and dog-like appearance made it an iconic animal, while surviving photographs, films, skins, skeletons and taxidermy specimens are now the only physical reminders of the species. That makes every previously undocumented specimen valuable to researchers. The rarity is especially striking among privately held material. ABC News reported that only 16 Tasmanian tiger specimens, including this newly confirmed mount, were held in private hands, with most of the remaining specimens in museum or university collections. The newly identified head could therefore provide researchers with information that cannot be obtained from photographs alone. Its skull may reveal individual variation in the species, while preserved tissue could potentially retain genetic material.Scientists want DNA from the newly discovered thylacineThe specimen has attracted interest from researchers involved in efforts to understand, and potentially one day revive, the extinct species. Andrew Pask, a University of Melbourne professor and chief biology officer at Colossal Biosciences, is among the scientists interested in examining the specimen. The team working on thylacine “de-extinction” hopes to collect DNA from the head. Researchers believe that sequencing DNA from additional thylacines could help build a better picture of the species' genetic diversity. Each individual genome can add information about differences between animals and the population as a whole. That information is particularly important for any future attempt to recreate aspects of the species' biology. A genetically diverse population would be far more viable than one based on a narrow genetic sample. However, the immediate scientific value of the specimen does not depend on de-extinction. A genuine thylacine skull is already an important historical and biological record.The strange taxidermy may have helped hide its true identityIronically, the very features that made the specimen look unconvincing may have helped it escape attention. Cranfield believes the mount's proportions were distorted by the amount of material packed beneath the skin. X-rays showed traditional taxidermy materials, including wood wool and tow, used to give the head its shape. The stuffing appears to have altered the proportions of the animal's face, while the unusual eyes and bulbous forehead made it look more like an eccentric fox mount than an extinct Tasmanian predator. Cranfield has said he would prefer to preserve the specimen largely in its existing condition rather than completely remount it. From his perspective, the imperfections are part of its history. That approach could also benefit researchers. Altering an old specimen risks destroying evidence about how it was originally prepared and preserved.A lost animal hiding in plain sightThe discovery is remarkable not simply because a thylacine specimen survived, but because it remained misidentified for so long. For years, the mounted head was apparently just another unusual piece of taxidermy. It entered an auction with a modest price estimate and was described as a fox. Only a collector's knowledge of animal anatomy revealed that something much more significant might be concealed beneath the skin. Now, the X-rays have settled the mystery. The head is a genuine thylacine, complete with an unusually well-preserved skull. Its next chapter is likely to involve researchers, DNA sampling and the International Thylacine Specimen Database rather than an ordinary collector's cabinet. For a species that has been extinct for almost 90 years, the discovery offers an unexpected new connection to an animal that has otherwise survived only in photographs, museum collections and historical records. What looked like a battered fox's head was, in fact, a piece of one of Australia's most famous extinct species, and its most important secret was hidden inside the skull.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Muslim law doesn’t allow elder brother to sell minor siblings’ land without court-appointed guardianship: Gauhati HC
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Gauhati high court has dismissed an appeal challenging a woman’s ownership of a piece of land she bought in 1975, saying the family mem.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Gauhati high court has dismissed an appeal challenging a woman’s ownership of a piece of land she bought in 1975, saying the family members who later challenged the sale were late in doing so. The court found that the sale was not valid for the shares belonging to the minor children, but said the woman had remained in possession of the land for more than 30 years. The judgment was pronounced on August 24, 2026.Why did the dispute arise?According to the court order, Tarubala Saha had bought 4 bigha, 2 katha and 10 lecha of land through a registered sale deed on February 18, 1975. The land originally belonged to Yad Ali, who had several children, some of whom were minors when he died.His son Nagar Ali sold the land to Saha, both for himself and on behalf of his four minor brothers and sisters.Saha claimed that she remained in possession of the land after buying it and had it cultivated through labourers. Her name was also entered in the land records. She alleged that the defendants removed her from the land on February 15, 2008 and built houses there.The defendants disputed the sale, saying Nagar Ali had no right to sell the shares belonging to his minor brothers and sisters. They also said he had not been appointed as their guardian by a court. They sought cancellation of the sale deed and claimed ownership of the land.The trial court ruled in Saha’s favour and ordered that she be given possession of the land. It also rejected the defendants’ claim. The first appeal filed by the defendants was later dismissed.Why did the high court uphold Saha’s claim?Justice Kalyan Rai Surana agreed with the lower courts that Nagar Ali could not legally sell the shares of his minor brothers and sisters simply because he was their elder brother. The court held that the sale was not valid for their four-fifths share. However, the sale was valid for Nagar Ali’s own one-fifth share.“Therefore, it is seen that the finding of the learned trial court, as modified by the finding by the learned first appellate court that the sale deed was void in respect of 4/5th share is the correct appreciation of Mohammedan Law, which does not recognize Nagar Ali, son of Yad Ali, who is also the elder brother of other four minor siblings, to act as their guardian so as to validly sell-off the land covered by the registered sale deed no. 2913/75 dated 18.02.1975,” the court noted.The court also found that Saha had been in possession of the land for around 30-33 years. People who had cultivated the land for her supported her claim, and their evidence was not shaken during questioning by the defendants’ lawyers.“Thus, the learned trial court is found to have correctly decided the issue no. 10 in the negative, meaning thereby that the sale deed no. 2913/75 dated 18.02.1975 (Ext.1) is valid. The said decision of the learned Trial Court has been affirmed by the learned First Appellate Court, by explaining that the said sale deed was valid so far as it relates to one-fifth share of Nagar Ali,” it further added.The high court further noted that Saha had proved her possession through people who cultivated the land for her. Their evidence remained unchallenged during cross-examination.“This court also concurs with the concurrent finding by the learned trial court and the learned first appellate court on issue nos. 7 and 10, because the plaintiff has been able to prove that she was in possession of the suit land since purchasing it and cultivating through adhiar, i.e. PW-3 and PW-5. The evidence of the PW-1, PW-3 and PW-5 remains impeached during cross-examination,” the court said.The high court noted that the defendants did not challenge the sale within the time allowed by law. They should have raised their claim within the prescribed period after becoming adults or after the land was handed over to Saha.The court said their long delay meant they could no longer seek cancellation of the sale deed or claim the land back.It also agreed with the lower courts that the defendants’ claim that they came to know about the sale only after receiving the court notice in 2008 was not believable.The High Court found no reason to interfere with the decisions of the two lower courts and dismissed the appeal with costs. It held that Saha’s successors were entitled to retain the benefit of her claim to the land and recover its possession.

articles.title: 16-year-old UP girl gang-raped inside moving bus during 47-km ride to Delhi's Kashmere Gate
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 16-year-old Class 11 student from Uttar Pradesh was allegedly gang-raped inside a moving sleeper bus after she boarded the vehicle seekin.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 16-year-old Class 11 student from Uttar Pradesh was allegedly gang-raped inside a moving sleeper bus after she boarded the vehicle seeking help while stranded in heavy rain, police said.The incident took place on the night of August 4 after the teenager, from Mainpuri district, left home following a disagreement with her family and set out to meet her cousin in Noida.According to police, the girl got off at Pari Chowk by mistake amid heavy rain and darkness. An empty sleeper bus passing through the area then stopped after she signalled for help.The driver, Kuldeep, and conductor, Sandeep, allegedly told her that the bus was headed towards Noida Sector 63 and allowed her to board.Police said the conductor allegedly began making obscene advances towards the teenager soon after the bus started moving. The girl has alleged that both the driver and conductor subsequently raped her and threatened to kill her when she resisted.The bus then travelled nearly 47 kilometres towards Kashmere Gate. The accused allegedly abandoned the teenager on Ring Road near the Kashmere Gate bus terminal late at night and fled.The terrified student approached Kashmere Gate police and reported the incident.Police subsequently arrested Kuldeep and Sandeep from a bus parking area in Timarpur and seized the sleeper bus. The vehicle has been sent for forensic examination.Investigators said the bus had earlier broken down and was taken to a workshop in Surajpur for repairs. After the repairs were completed, the driver and conductor were taking the empty bus to Timarpur when they encountered the teenager at Pari Chowk.Police said the sleeper bus had curtains around its berths, which allegedly helped the accused conceal what was happening inside during the journey.The bus covered around 47 kilometres between Pari Chowk and Kashmere Gate before the teenager was allegedly abandoned.Further investigation is underway.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: In 1934, Black cave guide Matt Bransford sold his 14-room Mammoth Cave hotel and land for just $3,000, far below market value; the family then moved 20 miles away as the national park took shape
articles.summary: US News: Deep below the forests of Kentucky is a world of water, stone and centuries-old human history. Mammoth Cave National Park has the world’s longest know.
articles.body: Deep below the forests of Kentucky is a world of water, stone and centuries-old human history. Mammoth Cave National Park has the world’s longest known cave system, but its story is about far more than underground passages. It’s also a story about indigenous exploration, enslaved guides, ambitious entrepreneurs, tourism, conservation, and families changed by the landscape’s transformation into a national park. One such story is that of Matt Bransford, a Black cave guide with family deep roots in Mammoth Cave and its tourism industry. Scroll down to read the story and what makes it so uniqueA cave with a history of thousands of yearsMammoth Cave is an incredible natural system, with more than 412 miles of mapped passages. Its limestone chambers and tunnels hold evidence of human activity for thousands of years. Before modern tourism was a thing, native Americans explored and mined the upper levels of the cave. Archeological finds include torches, pottery, woven objects, shells and other relics of early cave dwellers. Some groups entered the cave in search of minerals such as gypsum, selenite and other mineral deposits Later the cave became a major source of saltpeter. Some 400,000 pounds of the material were mined before and during the War of 1812 for the production of gunpowder.Legendary explorers with enslaved guidesIn the 19th century, as Mammoth Cave became a tourist attraction, African Americans were enslaved to serve as guides. In 1838, Franklin Gorin purchased the cave property and brought enslaved people to show visitors around. The following year when Dr John Croghan bought the cave he kept experienced guides who knew its winding passages.They were Stephen Bishop, Nick Bransford and Matt Bransford. Their knowledge of the cave was amazing. They guided visitors through difficult passages, found some previously unknown areas, and helped to build Mammoth Cave's reputation as a remarkable destination. Their contributions remain a significant part of the site’s history, especially as their expertise was developed under slavery.From tourism to growing community In the 19th century, the popularity of Mammoth Cave grew. Hotels, transportation networks and other businesses grew up around the attraction. From 1886 to 1929, the Mammoth Cave Railroad brought tourists to the cave and bolstered the local economy. Visitors could ride the rail to the Mammoth Cave Hotel, making it easier to get to the spot. The rising popularity of the cave also brought fierce competition. In the early 20th century many caves in the area were being promoted to tourists which led to what became known as the Kentucky Cave Wars.Matt Bransford and the new landscapeMatt Bransford was one of a number of generations of Black guides whose lives were closely tied to Mammoth Cave. His family remained engaged with the area’s tourism economy even as the region went through a period of major change. Bransford sold the 14-room Mammoth Cave hotel and land for $3,000 in 1934. The sale took place at a time when there was growing momentum for the creation of a national park and land was being bought up across the area. The Bransford family then moved some twenty miles away and the area around Mammoth Cave was slowly converted into a public park. Their story is one of a larger change. More and more land that had been private business, farms and communities, was being brought under the ownership of government to form the national park.Creating Mammoth Cave National ParkCreating the park was a massive land-acquisition effort. From about 600 land-owners, more than 45,000 acres had to be secured. In 1935, workers from the Civilian Conservation Corps arrived and started building roads, trails and other facilities. Much of the infrastructure that made the area a national park was put in place because of their efforts. Mammoth Cave National Park was officially established in 1941. It kept getting bigger and bigger. The cave and its surrounding landscape were designated as a World Heritage Site in 1981 and a Biosphere Reserve in 1990.A landscape where history and nature meetToday Mammoth Cave National Park conserves much more than its famous underground caverns. Forests, grasslands, rivers and karst landscapes are home to more than 1,300 plant species and many threatened or endangered species. The Green River, which flows through the park, is also famous for its incredible diversity of freshwater mussels. Here, visitors can hike, camp, ride bikes, canoes and horseback above ground. Historic sites, old churches and cemeteries and the remains of the area’s once-thriving communities, add another dimension to the story of the park. Of special interest is the Old Guide Cemetery. It is the resting place of cave guides, explorers and victims of the failed tuberculosis treatment experiment that was carried out inside the cave.A legacy preserved above and below groundThe tale of Mammoth Cave is ultimately a reminder that natural marvels are seldom free of human influence. Humans have explored its passages, used its resources, struggled over its future and built communities around it for thousands of years. That history is made all the more meaningful by the stories of people like Matt Bransford and other Black cave guides. Generations of visitors have come to experience a world hidden beneath the forests of Kentucky with their help. Today, Mammoth Cave is a geological wonder and a living historical record, where ancient artifacts, historic structures and sprawling natural landscapes tell a story that stretches far beyond the cave walls.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Women should stay confined to homes': Kerala Islamic scholar Kanthapuram defends purdah remark
articles.summary: KOCHI: Islamic scholar Kanthapuram A P Aboobacker Musliyar on Sunday said women should remain confined to their homes, days after a controversial circ.
articles.body: KOCHI: Islamic scholar Kanthapuram A P Aboobacker Musliyar on Sunday said women should remain confined to their homes, days after a controversial circular issued by the Kanthapuram faction of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama said women should not share public platforms with men.Speaking at an Islamic conference in Kochi, Kanthapuram defended the position, saying Islam had prescribed purdah for women to prevent what he described as “great destruction” caused by their presence on public platforms.“It is precisely recognising that bringing women onto public platforms in this manner causes great destruction that Islam mandated purdah for women. The Holy Quran states that women should live confined within their homes and must not make public appearances,” he said.The remarks came after the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama, the state's prominent council of Sunni-Shafi Islamic scholars, issued a circular last week stating that religious celebrations and programmes should remain within prescribed boundaries.In the circular, Samastha president E Sulaiman Musliyar and general secretary Kanthapuram directed that women should not share stages with men or appear in public spaces alongside them.The circular drew criticism from several quarters, including women political leaders who questioned the directive.Defending the stand, Kanthapuram said such views had been taught by religious scholars, particularly Samastha leaders, for around 100 years.“Therefore, you must understand that it is because all knowledgeable people, especially the leaders of Samastha, taught this here for 100 years that the women in this country have maintained their honour and dignity,” he said.Kanthapuram also said religious scholars who had studied Islam had an obligation to speak on the issue despite criticism.“When this is said, if leaders of any other organisation or Samastha leaders object to or question it, we have studied the religion and therefore have an obligation to say it. We will say it and continue to say it. No one can make us stop,” he said.(With PTI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news. articles.title: Navy commissions INS Nipun, boosts deep-sea diving & submarine rescue capability
articles.summary: News News: The Indian Navy has commissioned INS Nipun at the Naval Dockyard in Mumbai, marking the arrival of the second Diving Support Vessel in the indigenous .
articles.body: The Indian Navy has commissioned INS Nipun at the Naval Dockyard in Mumbai, marking the arrival of the second Diving Support Vessel in the indigenous Nistar-class, and completing a two-ship, two-coast capability for deep-sea diving, underwater intervention and submarine rescue. The commissioning ceremony was presided over by Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, Chief of Naval Staff. The commissioning has provided the Western fleet a dedicated diving support vessel to match sister ship INS Nistar, which has been operating out of the Eastern Naval Command since its own commissioning in July last year.Built by Hindustan Shipyard Limited at Visakhapatnam, Nipun was delivered to the Navy on 30 July this year following an extensive round of outfitting and sea trials. The contract for both vessels was signed with HSL back in September 2018 for a combined cost of around Rs 2,393 crore, with keels laid for Nistar in December 2019 and for the Nipun three months later. The Sanskrit name Nipun, meaning one who is adept and well-versed in a particular discipline.At roughly 118 metres in length and displacing over 8,500 tonnes, Nipun carries close to 75% indigenous content, demonstrating India's growing ability to design and construct technologically sophisticated naval platforms domestically. The ship is built to support saturation diving operations at depths of up to 300 metres, alongside side-stage diving capability extending to 75 metres, making it suited for both submarine rescue and the inspection, maintenance and repair of critical underwater infrastructure such as subsea cables and pipelines. A 15-tonne subsea crane, dynamic positioning systems and Remotely Operated Vehicles capable of working at depths up to 1,000 metres.Central to Nipun's role is its function as a mother ship for Deep Submergence Rescue Vehicles, the specialised submersibles that can dock directly with a stricken submarine's escape hatch to extract the trapped crew in the event of an emergency. The ship also carries an eight-bed hospital, an intensive care unit, an operating theatre and hyperbaric medical facilities, providing the vessel the ability to handle the very specific in nature ability to handle deep sea diving related medical issues. With INS Nistar already having tested this rescue architecture during Exercise Pacific Reach off Singapore last September, Nipun's induction mirrors that capability on India's western seaboard, giving the navy a genuinely two-coast submarine rescue and deep-sea intervention capability for the first time.
